messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: CDF and CCDF exceptions or 0/1 returns?
parts:
Daniel, Rob and I discussed this issue and concluded that what we want
is to have CDFs and CCDFs throw exceptions if there are inputs outside
of support of the corresponding density.

Example 1: closed support interval

uniform_cdf(y, L, U);

support is [L,U]

if y not in [L,U] throw an exception


Example 2: open support interval

lognormal_cdf(y, mu, sigma);

support is (0,inf)

if y not in (0,inf), throw an exception (that is, throw on 0 or +inf)

Is this OK with everyone?

The alternative is obviously to have CDFs return 0 for y below support and
1 for y above support. We thought having the exceptions would help users diagnose
problems more easily.

- Bob

messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] CDF and CCDF exceptions or 0/1 returns?
parts:
I'm not convinced this is the best.  For one, CDFs and CCDFs are well defined outside the support of their corresponding PDFs.  I agree it's good to catch bounds violations when used in truncated sampling statements, but there are other uses for CDF functions where returning a valid value outside the bounds might be the expected and reasonable behaviour.  I'd suggest instead that we simply add bounds checks as part of truncated sampling statements, probably before even calling the PDF.

At any rate, I won't argue this point strongly, just my $0.02CAD or $0.05BRL since I'm Brazil at the moment...

Cheers,
Marcus

That's a good question. Right now, the discrete CDFs only
take integer arguments. That does leave open the issue
of having numbers outside of support, as in a negative
integer for a binomial or one above the total count.

We also have to be careful as discussed before that the
gradients are zero in areas outside the support.

messages.author: 89abf8a3796a510b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] CDF and CCDF exceptions or 0/1 returns?
parts:
It seems like whatever we decide for evaluating CDFs/CMFs, log densities should have the same behavior. Currently, our treatment of restricted support distributions isn't consistent. For instance, beta_log throws a domain error if any y > 1 or y < 0, but lognormal_log returns negative infinity.

My vote is to throw exceptions.


Rob
On Sat, Dec 20, 2014 at 3:15 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

I think if someone wants to evaluate a (C)CMF at non-integer values, they can use floor() explicitly. And if so, then I think anything outside the support should be an error because the user could check whether the value is within the support before calling the (C)CDF.

Ben


On Saturday, December 20, 2014 10:30:11 AM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
Although I can envisage reasons for evaluating (C)CDFs at
non-integer values, I can’t think of a reason for evaluating
them outside of their support.  Even if there are some
obscure reasons I’m with Ben that most cases would be
mistakes and so I favor the more conservative approach
of throwing exceptions outside of the support (and
possibly at non-integer values, although less so).

On Dec 19, 2014, at 3:03 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> That's a good question.  Right now, the discrete CDFs only
> take integer arguments.  That does leave open the issue
> of having numbers outside of support, as in a negative
> integer for a binomial or one above the total count.
>
> We also have to be careful as discussed before that the
> gradients are zero in areas outside the support.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Dec 19, 2014, at 2:50 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> Relatedly, what should we do with CMFs or CCMFs when someone evaluates it at a non-integer? Mathematically, they are still well-defined, but it is likely to be a mistake if done in Stan.
>>
>> Ben
>>
>> On Friday, December 19, 2014 12:15:22 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> The current code isn't consistent on the behavior.
>>
>> I'm OK with having them return 0 below their support and 1
>> above their support as long as we do it consistently for
>> all the CDFs and CCDFs.
>>
>> Does anyone else have an opinion?  Or an example where
>> you'd use an input to a CDF or CCDF outside of its support?
>>
>> Marco --- it was issue #1142 that kicked up this discussion
>> again.  I don't remember documenting it anywhere, so I'll
>> add the final decision to the manual.
>>
>> - Bob
>>
>>> On Dec 18, 2014, at 10:23 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>>
>>> I'm not convinced this is the best.  For one, CDFs and CCDFs are well defined outside the support of their corresponding PDFs.  I agree it's good to catch bounds violations when used in truncated sampling statements, but there are other uses for CDF functions where returning a valid value outside the bounds might be the expected and reasonable behaviour.  I'd suggest instead that we simply add bounds checks as part of truncated sampling statements, probably before even calling the PDF.
>>>
>>> At any rate, I won't argue this point strongly, just my $0.02CAD or $0.05BRL since I'm Brazil at the moment...
>>>
>>> Cheers,
>>> Marcus
>>>
>>>
>>> On Thu, Dec 18, 2014 at 6:32 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>> We had this discussion previously and I believe we settled on the latter strategy which is how they're currently implemented.  I'm fine with changing that behavior to make the behavior more in line with other bounds.
>>>
>>>> On Dec 18, 2014, at 5:50 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>>>>
>>>> Daniel, Rob and I discussed this issue and concluded that what we want
>>>> is to have CDFs and CCDFs throw exceptions if there are inputs outside
>>>> of support of the corresponding density.
>>>>
>>>> Example 1:  closed support interval
>>>>
>>>>  uniform_cdf(y, L, U);
>>>>
>>>>  support is [L,U]
>>>>
>>>>  if y not in [L,U] throw an exception
>>>>
>>>>
>>>> Example 2:  open support interval
>>>>
>>>>  lognormal_cdf(y, mu, sigma);
>>>>
>>>>  support is (0,inf)
>>>>
>>>>  if y not in (0,inf), throw an exception (that is, throw on 0 or +inf)
>>>>
>>>> Is this OK with everyone?
>>>>
>>>> The alternative is obviously to have CDFs return 0 for y below support and
>>>> 1 for y above support.  We thought having the exceptions would help users diagnose
>>>> problems more easily.
>>>>
>>>> - Bob
